vignette:
Anwar Khan sits with a stillness that seems at odds with the tension in his hands, which are clasped so tightly on his knees that the knuckles are white. He came to the clinic at the firm insistence of his son, Tariq, after an incident involving a dropped pot in the garden. For most of his 79 years, Mr. Khan has defined himself by his capacity for hard work and his quiet stoicism, qualities that are now failing him in the disquieting silence of retirement.

His story begins in 1971, when he was a young soldier, barely twenty, caught in the maelstrom of the Bangladesh Liberation War. He doesn't speak of battles or skirmishes. His memory, the one that returns unbidden, is of a marketplace in a small town. It was a sweltering afternoon, the air thick with the smell of overripe mangoes, diesel fumes, and dust. He was on patrol, his rifle a heavy, foreign object in his hands, when the explosion tore through the fabric of the day. He remembers the sound not as a bang, but as a deep, guttural *whump* that seemed to suck the air from his lungs. Then came the screaming. What haunts him most is not the carnage itself, but a single, vivid image: a woman's vibrant yellow sari, splayed in the dirt, covered in a fine red mist. He stood frozen for a moment that stretched into an eternity, paralyzed by the sheer wrongness of it all.

He emigrated a few years later, seeking a life scrubbed clean of that past. He found it, or so he thought, in the cavernous, echoing spaces of a warehouse. For forty-five years, he worked the forklift, stacking pallets with a precision that bordered on art. The roar of the machinery was a welcome anesthetic, loud enough to drown out the chatter in his head. The physical exhaustion at the end of each twelve-hour shift was a blessing, a heavy blanket that smothered the nightmares before they could fully form. He was a good worker, reliable and solitary.

His marriage buckled under the strain of the silence he carried. His ex-wife, Safiya, used to plead with him to talk, to tell her what ghosts kept him staring at the ceiling all night. But the words were locked away, and he didn't have the key. He couldn't explain the sudden, searing rage that would boil up when a car backfired, or why he had to check the locks on the doors three times before bed. He saw her love curdle into frustration, then resignation. When she left, a part of him felt a grim sense of relief. It was one less person to fail. He raised his son with a quiet, gruff affection, a love expressed through providing, not through presence.

Retirement was supposed to be a reward, a time to tend his prized rose garden and enjoy his grandchildren. Instead, it has been a reckoning. Without the warehouse's noise and exhaustion, the past has rushed into the vacuum. The silence of his small suburban home is now more deafening than any forklift. Last week, when his daughter-in-law dropped a ceramic pot, the sharp crack sent him diving to the patio floor, hands over his head, the smell of potting soil and terracotta momentarily replacing the memory of dust and blood. He saw the fear and confusion in his family's eyes, and for the first time, the shame was sharper than the fear.

He avoids the news, especially stories from the Middle East or South Asia. He no longer goes to the bustling international grocery store on Saturdays, the crush of people and the shouting of vendors too much to bear. He knows he loves his grandchildren, but the feeling is distant, an intellectual fact rather than a felt warmth. He watches them play as if through a thick pane of glass, their laughter muffled and far away. At night, he wakes up drenched in sweat, the image of a yellow sari burning behind his eyelids. The man who prided himself on his strength now feels brittle, a hollowed-out version of himself, terrified of the next loud noise that might shatter him completely.
